\subsection*{Problem 1}

Suppose you have a sample $Y_1,Y_2...,Y_n$ drawn with replacement from a population with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.

Consider the following estimator for $\mu$: $\tilde{Y} = \frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i$

\subsubsection*{Part A}

What is $E[\tilde{Y}]$?

\bigskip

\color{red}

$$E[\tilde{Y}] = E[\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i]$$ $$= \frac{1}{2n} E[\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i]$$

$$= \frac{1}{2n} \sum_{i=1}^n E[Y_i]$$ by linearity of expectations

$$= \frac{1}{2n} \sum_{i=1}^n E[Y]$$ by IID

$$= \frac{1}{2n} \sum_{i=1}^n \mu$$ by definition

$$= \frac{1}{2n} n \mu$$

$$= \frac{n}{2n} \mu$$

$$= \frac{1}{2} \mu$$

\color{black}

\subsubsection*{Part B}

How does $E[\tilde{Y}]$ compare to $E[\bar{Y}]$? (where $\bar{Y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i$)

Should we just ask for bias calculation? 

\bigskip

\color{red} similar steps show that $E[\bar{Y}] = \mu$. $\bar{Y}$ is unbiased, $\tilde{Y}$ is biased; bias does not change in $n$ \color{black}

\subsubsection*{Part C}

Showing your work, calculate $Var[\tilde{Y}]$.

\bigskip

\color{red}

$$Var[\tilde{Y}] = V[\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i]$$

$$ = (\frac{1}{2n})^2 V[\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i]$$

$$ = (\frac{1}{2n})^2 \sum_{i=1}^n V[Y]$$ because IID, covariances are 0

$$ = (\frac{1}{2n})^2 \sum_{i=1}^n \sigma^2$$ by definition

$$ = (\frac{1}{2n})^2 n \sigma^2$$

$$ = \frac{n}{(2n)^2} \sigma^2$$

$$ = \frac{1}{4n} \sigma^2$$

```{=tex}
\color{black}
\subsubsection*{Part D}
```
How does $Var[\tilde{Y}]$ compare to $Var[\bar{Y}]$?

\bigskip

\color{red}

Similar steps show that $V[\bar{Y}] = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}$

$\frac{1}{n} > \frac{1}{4n}$ so our $\tilde{Y}$ estimator has a lower variance than the sample mean. But the estimator is biased, so we probably wouldn't want to use it over the mean.

\color{black}

\subsection*{Problem 2}

Suppose we have a sample of $Y_1 \ldots Y_n$ and binary $X_1 \ldots X_n$ stored in an \textbf{R} dataframe \`df' with $n$ rows. We run this code.

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(ggplot2)
n <- 500
x <- c(rep(0,n/2),rep(1,n/2))
set.seed(220220)
y <- 2.6*x +  rnorm(n) + runif(n,-1,1)


df <- data.frame(y,x)



q2<- ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_jitter(width=.25) +
  geom_hline(yintercept=mean(df$y[df$x==0]), linetype="dashed")+ 
   geom_hline(yintercept=mean(df$y[df$x==1]), linetype="dashed")+ 
  xlab("x") +
  ylab("y") +
  theme_bw() 

```

```{r}
#| echo: true
B=10000
theta<- rep(NA,B)
for( b in 1:B ){
bootind = sample(1:n,size=n,replace=T)
dfboot = df[bootind,]
theta[b]<- (mean(dfboot$y[dfboot$x==1])-mean(dfboot$y[dfboot$x==0]))
}
```

```{r}
#| out-height: 3.5in
#| fig-ncol: 2
#| fig-subcap:
#|  -  Histogram of the vector Y's elements
#|  -  Jittered Scatterplot of X and Y
ggplot() + geom_histogram(aes(x=y,     y=after_stat(density)), alpha=.3) + 
           geom_vline(aes(xintercept=mean(y)), alpha=.5) + 
           geom_vline(aes(xintercept=mean(y)+c(-1,1)*sd(y)), linetype='dashed', alpha=.5) + 
           geom_pointrange(aes(x=mean(y), xmin=mean(y)-1.96*sd(y), xmax=mean(y)+1.96*sd(y), y=.025)) + theme_bw() + xlab('') + ylab('')

q2 
```

```{r}
#| out-height: 3.5in
#| fig-ncol: 2
#| fig-subcap:
#|  -  Histogram of the theta's elements

ggplot() + geom_histogram(aes(x=theta, y=after_stat(density)), alpha=.3) + 
           geom_vline(aes(xintercept=mean(theta)), alpha=.5) + 
           geom_vline(aes(xintercept=mean(theta)+c(-1,1)*sd(theta)), linetype='dashed', alpha=.5) + 
           geom_pointrange(aes(x=mean(theta), xmin=mean(theta)-1.96*sd(theta), xmax=mean(theta)+1.96*sd(theta), y=.25)) + theme_bw() + xlab('') + ylab('')
```

\subsection*{Problem 3}

Consider the following data set with treatment $d$, covariate $x$, and outcome $y$, which has been fit with a linear interactive model. Note that the treated units with $d=1$ are denoted as triangles, while the control units with $d=0$ are denoted with circles. The regression line for the treated units is solid, while the regression line for the control units is dashed.

```{r}
x <- c(0,2,4,0,0,2,4,4)
y <- c(2,4,6,12.25,8,5.25,3.25,1)
d <- c(1,1,1,0,0,0,0,0)
#plot(x,y,pch=c(19,19,19,1,1,1,1,1))
#abline(lm(y[d==0] ~x[d==0]),lty=2)
#abline(lm(y[d==1] ~x[d==1]))

df<- data.frame(x=x,y=y,d=d)
m1<- lm(y[d==0] ~x[d==0],data=df)
m2<- lm(y[d==1] ~x[d==1], data=df)
plot<- ggplot(data = df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point(aes(shape=as.factor(d)),size=2) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 13, by = 1)) + geom_abline(slope=m1$coef[2], intercept=m1$coef[1], linetype="dashed")+geom_abline(slope=m2$coef[2], intercept=m2$coef[1])

plot + theme(legend.position="none")
```

\subsubsection*{Part A}

Fill in the table with potential outcomes based on the observed data. Put a question mark (?) in the cells for which you do not have data.

\subsubsection*{Part B}

What is the probability of receiving treatment for males? What is the probability of receiving treatment for females?

\color{red}

$P(D=1|Male) = \frac{1}{4}$

$P(D=1|Female) = \frac{1}{2}$ \color{black}

\subsubsection*{Part C}

What is the treatment effect among males? What is the treatment effect among females?

\color{red}

Males: $20 - \frac{5+10+5}{3} = 20 - \frac{20}{3} = 13.333$

Females: $\frac{10+5+10+5}{4} - \frac{5+0+5+5}{4} = \frac{30}{4} - \frac{15}{4} = 7.5 - 3.75 = 3.75$ \color{black}

\subsubsection*{Part D}

If you ignored the conditional randomization and calculated the average treatment effect without accounting for sex, what would your estimate be?

\color{red}

$\frac{20+10+5+10+5}{5} - \frac{5+10+5+5+0+5+5}{7} = \frac{50}{5} - \frac{35}{7} = 10 - 5 = 5$ \color{black}

\subsubsection*{Part E}

To analyze our data, we are interested in fitting the following model: $$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \beta_2 Sex_i + \beta_3 D_i:Sex_i$$ where $Sex_i =1$ for males and $=0$ for females. Fill in the table below using $\beta$s

```{=tex}
\hline
```

\subsection*{Problem 7}

\subsubsection*{Part A}

Suppose we want $\beta_1$ from $y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \beta_2 z_i + \beta_3 x_i:z_i + e_i$ but we run the regression $lm (y\sim x)$ without $z$ or the interaction term. We have de-meaned our variables $x_i$ and $z_i$ such that $\bar{x}=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i =0$ and $\bar{z}=\sum_{i=1}^n z_i =0$. Derive what your coefficient on $x$ from $lm (y\sim x)$, which is $\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 }$, will be in terms of $\beta$s and justify your steps. Hint: you can relabel $x_i:z_i$ as a different variable.

\bigskip

\color{red}

The coefficient on $x$ from $lm (y\sim x)$ is $$\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 }$$

Plug in $y_i$ defined by the multivariate regression: $y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \beta_2 z_i + \beta_3 x_i: z_i+ e_i$

Let's redefine $x_i:z_i = w_i$

$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \beta_2 z_i + \beta_3 w_i + e_i$

$$\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \beta_2 z_i +  \beta_3 w_i + e_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 }$$

Distribute

$$\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \beta_0 }{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \beta_1 x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \beta_2 z_i }{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \beta_3 w_i }{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 }+  \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i  e_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 }$$ Let's work through each term.

$$\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \beta_0 }{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } = \frac{ \beta_0 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i }{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } = \frac{ \beta_0 *0 }{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } = 0$$

as $x$ is demeaned, $\sum x_i =0$

\bigskip

$$\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \beta_1 x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } = \frac{  \beta_1 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } = \beta_1$$

\bigskip

$$\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \beta_2 z_i }{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } = \frac{\beta_2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i z_i }{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 }$$

\bigskip

$$\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \beta_3 w_i }{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } = \frac{\beta_3 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i w_i }{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 }$$

\bigskip

$$\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i  e_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } = \frac{0}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } =0$$ we know that $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i e_i =0$ from the first order conditions on our least squares estimator (we chose the intercept and coefficient(s) that minimize the sum of squared residuals)

\bigskip

Thus we have

$$\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } = \beta_1 + \frac{\beta_2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i z_i }{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } + \frac{\beta_3 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i w_i }{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 }$$ Plugging back in for $w_i$, $$\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } = \beta_1 + \frac{\beta_2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i z_i }{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 } + \frac{\beta_3 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i z_i x_i }{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 }$$

\color{black}


\subsubsection*{Part A}

```{r}
#| echo: false

p3n <- 200
z <- c(rep(0,p3n/2),rep(1,p3n/2))
set.seed(220220)
x <-   rnorm(p3n,mean=1,sd=1) + z*rnorm(p3n,mean=3,sd = 1)
y <- 12 + (-3)*x + (4)*z + 8*x*z + rnorm(p3n) + runif(p3n,-4,6)


dfp3 <- data.frame(y,x,z)

q1 <- ggplot(data = dfp3, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = factor(z)),size = 1,alpha=.5) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(1,19), label = c("z=0","z=1")) +
  xlab("x") +
  ylab("y") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.box.just = "left",
        legend.justification = c("left","top"),
        legend.position = c(0,1),
        legend.margin = margin(6,6,6,6),
        legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.box.background = element_rect(color="black",size=1))

q2<- ggplot(data = dfp3, aes(x = x, y = z)) +
  geom_jitter(height=.25) +  xlab("x") +
  ylab("z") +
  theme_bw()



modone<- lm(y~x+z+x:z,data=dfp3)
modtwo<- lm(z ~ x, data=dfp3)
modthree<- lm(x*z ~ x,data=dfp3)
modfour<- lm(y~x,data=dfp3)
```
